prospect.name: Shyam
prospect.location: United Kingdom (relocated from India approximately one year ago)
prospect.training_background: Former endurance cyclist — longest ride 600 km over 2-3 days roughly 4 years ago, most recent long ride 200 km. Previously followed a coached program via the FITTR app 2-3 years ago and lost about 10 kg while calorie counting. Trained with dumbbells and barbells at home. Since relocating to the UK a year ago the only activity is walking about 1.5 miles four days a week to the office plus an occasional one-mile walk after dinner. No bicycle at present, one is on order. No gym membership yet.
prospect.medical: Self-reported pre-diabetic at his last health check, which was over a year ago before he moved to the UK; diet unchanged since. History of elbow pain that arose during weight training and led him to stop lifting and then to stop training entirely.

signals: Explicitly lost ground he once had: "during that program, I was able to get into good shape... but somewhere up there, I lost it"
Wants a former self back — restarting cycling, ordered a bike, "I think I have to bring back that discipline again"
Regret framing around a derailment rather than a plateau: "I've deviated and derailed. Right now, I want to come back to track"
Not the skeptical_bargain_hunter despite the price resistance — he did not argue value against a cheaper substitute, he simply could not fund the number

goals.text: Get back into good shape and look better
Reverse pre-diabetes and avoid progressing to type 2 diabetes
Restart cycling and test his limits again on endurance rides
Rebuild the discipline and routine he had during his earlier coached program
Stay well enough to keep up with and set an example for his nine-year-old son

pains.text: Stopped training entirely after elbow pain, and never restarted — three years off
Pre-diabetic on his last blood work, with no follow-up check in over a year
Elbow pain during weight training that made him reduce load and then quit lifting
Carb-heavy home diet with no calorie tracking since he stopped his old program
Relocation to the UK removed his bike, his home weights and his gym, and he has not chosen a replacement
Lost motivation once he could not lift, and let everything else fall away with it

objections.raw_quote: Okay. So I don't think I will be able to manage that 4,500 for six months.
objections.rep_response: Did not isolate the objection, asked no financial-picture questions and offered no payment plan. Immediately abandoned the $6,000 program and pivoted to a $200/month community subscription: "I don't want to leave you with nothing. There is one way."

objections.raw_quote: to be frank, I was never ready for this kind of package, monetarily 6,000, 4,000, whatever, for a six month program. So I'm not ready for that.
objections.rep_response: Conceded the main offer entirely and redirected to the smaller subscription: "Yeah, I'm not talking about the 6,000. I'm talking about the, you know, the smaller investment."

objections.raw_quote: Oh, maybe I have to think about it.
objections.rep_response: Asked "what are your thoughts on this, like, exactly?" but ran none of the scripted think-about-it moves, then accepted "let me go through that" and agreed to email a link.

tiers.note: One-to-one coaching with Trevor. Also quoted live in sterling as "4,500 pounds".

Off-menu downsell — community access with the kettlebell movement library, a structured three-month progressive-overload program, a weekly group coaching call with Trevor and his nutrition protocol. Subscription, cancel any time.

evidence: Explicit no to the core offer: "That's way out of my league" and "I was never ready for this kind of package... So I'm not ready for that."
No payment taken, no payment link sent on the call — only an offer to email details.

Counter-evidence: the conversation is not fully dead. The prospect asked "is there an app or something where I need to subscribe?" and agreed to review the material — "let me go through that, and I can tell you much more."
Counter-evidence: what remains open is a $200/month subscription, not the $6,000 program, so the sales opportunity as defined is lost even if the subscription later converts.
outcome.next_step: Rep to email a link to the $200/month community subscription; prospect to review it and respond.

notable.note: The $6,000 offer was abandoned within about ninety seconds of the first price reaction, with no isolation, no financial-picture questions and no payment plan discussed — the exact sequence the rep's manager coached him on in the 1-1 recorded the same day. In its place the rep improvised a $200/month community subscription that is not part of the stated offer. Separately, the rep used an unqualified mortality claim ("they might not even get to the 55th birthday") on a prospect who had just disclosed pre-diabetes, and never asked whether any clinician had cleared him to train.

quality.notes: Frequent inversion. Questions clearly belonging to the rep appear at the tail of the prospect's turns ("Are you doing that right now?" at 00:04:38, "Have you tried them before?" at 00:08:07, "Do you have access to like a local gym?" at 00:08:09). The exchange from 00:11:19 to 00:11:58 is inverted wholesale — the answers about the checkup date and about having a nine-year-old son are labelled as the rep. Roles were reconstructed from content throughout.
